fetched_contents.text: Aortic Stenosis - StatPearls Continuing Education Activity Aortic stenosis is a common valvular disorder, especially in the elderly population, causing left ventricular outflow obstruction. Etiologies include congenital (bicuspid/unicuspid), calcific, and rheumatic disease. Symptoms such as exertional dyspnea or fatigue gradually develop after a long asymptomatic latent period of about 10 to 20 years. Patients go on to develop chest pain, heart failure, and syncope. This activity outlines the evaluation and treatment of aortic stenosis and highlights the interprofessional team's role in evaluating and treating patients with this condition. Objectives: * Identify the etiology of aortic stenosis. * Outline the appropriate evaluation of aortic stenosis. * Review the indications for different types of management options available for aortic stenosis. * Describe interprofessional team strategies for improving communication and care coordination to advance the aortic stenosis condition. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic. Introduction Aortic stenosis is a common valvular disorder leading to left ventricular outflow obstruction.[1] The anterograde velocity across the valve must be at least 2 m/sec, whereas aortic valve sclerosis is the thickening and calcification without a significant pressure gradient. Etiologies include congenital (bicuspid/unicuspid), calcific, and rheumatic disease. Symptoms such as exertional dyspnea or fatigue gradually develop after a long asymptomatic latent period of about 10 to 20 years. Patients go on to develop chest pain, heart failure, and syncope. The definitive treatment for aortic stenosis includes aortic valve replacement, either via a surgical or percutaneous approach. Survival is excellent during the asymptomatic phase, but mortality is more than 90% within a few years after the onset of symptoms.[2][3][4][5][6][7] Etiology Congenital A congenitally abnormal valve with superimposed calcification can cause aortic stenosis.[8] The bicuspid aortic valve is the most common cause of aortic stenosis in patients less than the age of 70 years in developed countries. Acquired Rheumatic valve disease is the most common cause in developing countries.[8] The commissures of the leaflets fuse to leave a small central orifice. Other causes include calcification of the tri-leaflet valve, alkaptonuria, systemic lupus erythematosus, ochronosis, irradiation, homozygous type II lipoproteinemia, and metabolic diseases such as Fabry disease.[9][10] Mineral metabolism disturbances, such as end-stage renal disease, have also been shown to contribute to the calcification of the valve.[11] Obstruction to the left ventricular (LV) outflow can occur above or below the valve, causing supravalvular stenosis and subvalvular stenosis, respectively. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can cause dynamic subvalvular stenosis. Epidemiology The prevalence of calcific aortic sclerosis is about 1% to 2% in patients aged 65 or less and 29% in patients aged 65 or more. About 2 to 9% of patients aged greater than 75 have severe aortic stenosis.[12][13] The prevalence of aortic sclerosis ranges from 9 to 45% in patients with a mean age of 54 to 81 and increases with age.[14] The relative prevalence of aortic stenosis in patients with tri-leaflet versus congenitally abnormal valves varies with age.[15] The causes of aortic stenosis vary geographically as calcific stenosis is more common in North America and Europe, while rheumatic valve disease is more common in developing countries. The number is expected to increase twofold or threefold in the coming decades with the aging of the population.[16] Pathophysiology Left ventricular (LV) obstruction caused by the stenosis of the valve increases LV systolic pressure. It also results in increased LV ejection time (LVET), decreased aortic pressure, and increased LV end-diastolic pressure. The increased afterload, in addition, to an increase in LV volume overload, leads to an increase in LV mass, ultimately leading to LV dysfunction and failure. Myocardial oxygen consumption increases with increased LV systolic pressure, LV mass, and LVET, while myocardial perfusion time decreases with increased LVET. Hence, LV function further deteriorates with increased myocardial oxygen consumption and decreased myocardial oxygen supply.[8] History and Physical The acquired aortic stenosis manifests with exertional dyspnea, syncope, angina, and, ultimately, heart failure.[17][18] Typically, symptoms begin at the age of 50 to 70 years in patients with the bicuspid aortic valve and in greater than 70 years in patients with tri-leaflet valve calcific stenosis. Patients progressively experience a gradual decrease in exercise tolerance, dyspnea on exertion, and fatigue. Severe exertional dyspnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, and pulmonary edema show various degrees of pulmonary venous hypertension. Angina results from the combination of the need for increased oxygen in hypertrophied myocardium and reduction of oxygen delivery secondary to the excessive compression of coronary vessels. Syncope is caused by the decrease in cerebral perfusion occurring during exertion when the arterial pressure declines due to systemic vasodilation and an inadequate increase in cardiac output related to stenosis. It is also due to the malfunction of the baroreceptor mechanism in severe aortic stenosis. Non-cardiac symptoms include gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding and cerebral emboli. GI bleeding is observed in patients with severe aortic stenosis and is often associated with angiodysplasia or other vascular malformations. It manifests from shear stress-induced platelet aggregation and reduction in the von Willebrand factor.[19] Cerebral emboli occur due to microthrombi formation on thickened bicuspid valves. fetched_contents.text: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) - Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) ---------------------------------------- What is transcatheter aortic valve replacement? Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), also known as TAVR or transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), is a procedure to treat aortic stenosis, a narrowing of the aortic valve. The narrowing blocks the flow of blood to your body and forces your heart to work harder. This causes symptoms such as chest pain and shortness of breath. TAVR replaces an aortic valve that is not working properly or is diseased with an aortic valve made from animal tissue. The TAVR procedure is minimally invasive, requiring only a small cut in the skin. It does not require open-heart surgery. The aortic valve is one of four valves that control blood flow in the heart. The aortic valve specifically controls the blood that runs from the heart through your aorta and to the rest of the body. Over time or because of a congenital heart defect, you can develop aortic stenosis, a type of heart valve disease. Your healthcare provider may explain risks and benefits of both TAVR and open-heart surgery. This information will help you decide which one is better for your specific needs. How it works There are several ways your doctor can perform TAVR, depending on your health and the health of your blood vessels. * A TAVR using the femoral artery, a blood vessel in your groin or thigh, is the most common. Your doctor guides a tube with the replacement valve through the femoral artery to the heart. * Blood vessels in the chest may be used by the doctor to guide the tube to your heart if your femoral artery is too small or damaged. This approach is called transapical access. * Stomach area blood vessels may be used for TAVR if a patient’s leg arteries are too small or diseased for a more standard approach. NHLBI researchers developed this approach, called transcaval access, to make TAVR available to high-risk patients. It is less common. The doctor makes holes in both the vena cava, a major vein in your stomach area, and the nearby aorta to feed the tube with the replacement valve first through the vein and then through the aorta to the heart. You may be able to stay awake during this procedure. This type of TAVR approach may benefit women, who often have smaller blood vessels than men. * Accessing the heart from the vessel under the clavicle, or collar bone, may be an option if you have had heart surgery before or if you have another condition that makes it difficult to access other parts of the chest. * Your doctor may use the carotid artery in the neck to feed the tube to the heart — called transcarotid access. This type of procedure is rare but may be used when other options will not work. * Another rare location is through the septum, the wall of tissue that separates the right and left atria of the heart. Your doctor reaches the damaged valve by guiding the tube through a blood vessel from your thigh to the heart. New approaches to TAVR are making the procedure available to more people. As with any medical procedure, there are certain risks associated with a TAVR procedure. In some patients, a replacement valve can push aside an old valve flap, blocking blood flow to the heart. The result — coronary artery obstruction — is a rare but life-threatening complication of TAVR. NHLBI researchers have invented a technique called the BASILICA procedure to prevent it. Learn about NHLBI's TAVR research. What to expect during the procedure Cardiologists, or doctors who specialize in the heart, typically perform TAVR in a hospital. Before TAVR, your healthcare providers will measure the valve opening, then give you medicines that relax you or put you to sleep, as well as medicines to prevent dangerous blood clots . During the procedure, your doctor will guide a thin, flexible tube called a catheter to your heart through blood vessels they can access from your groin or thigh, stomach area, chest, neck, or collar bone. Inside the catheter is a folded replacement valve, which is placed securely within the old valve. Once your doctor is sure the new valve has been placed correctly, they will check for leaks and possible complications, such as a problem in the heart’s electrical signaling. What to expect after the procedure After a TAVR procedure, your hospital stay may be just a few days depending on the approach used. You may be able to return to daily activities, such as exercising and driving, in just a few weeks. However, as with any procedure involving the heart and blood vessels, TAVR carries some risks both during and after surgery, including: * Damage and bleeding where the catheters were inserted * Injury to the kidneys or the heart * Leaking in the new valve because it does not fit well * Need for a permanent pacemaker due to damage to the heart’s electrical signaling during the procedure * Stroke You may get medicine to prevent infection or abnormal blood clots. About a month after the procedure, your provider will do tests to check how well the valve is working and how well you are healing. You may need follow-up visits every year to make sure the valve continues working as it should.

fetched_contents.text: 5-Year Outcomes After Transcatheter or Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement in Low-Risk Patients With Aortic Stenosis Central Illustration Abstract Background The Evolut Low Risk trial demonstrated that transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) was noninferior to surgery for the primary endpoint of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke at 2 years. Outcomes at 5 years have not been reported. Objectives This study sought to evaluate 5-year clinical and hemodynamic outcomes with TAVR vs surgery in patients from the Evolut Low Risk trial. Methods We randomly assigned low-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis to TAVR or surgery. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke. Secondary endpoints included clinical, echocardiographic, and quality-of-life outcomes through 5 years. Results A total of 1,414 patients underwent an attempted implant (n = 730 TAVR, n = 684 surgery). The mean age was 74 years (range 51-88 years), and women accounted for 35% of patients. At 5 years the Kaplan-Meier estimate for the primary endpoint of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke was 15.5% for the TAVR group and 16.4% for the surgery group (P = 0.47). The Kaplan-Meier estimates in the TAVR and surgery groups for all-cause mortality were 13.5% and 14.9% (P = 0.39) and for disabling stroke were 3.6% and 4.0% (P = 0.57). Cardiovascular mortality was 7.2% in the TAVR group and 9.3% in the surgery group (P = 0.15). Noncardiovascular mortality in the TAVR group was 6.8% and 6.2% in the surgery group (P = 0.73). A site-level vital status sweep was performed for patients who were lost to follow-up or withdrew from the study. With the addition of these patients, the all-cause mortality rate at 5 years for patients undergoing TAVR was 14.7% and for surgery was 15.2% (P = 0.74). Over 5 years, valve reintervention rate was 3.3% for TAVR and 2.5% for surgery (P = 0.44). A sustained improvement in quality of life was observed in both treatment arms with mean Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire summary score of 88.3 ± 15.8 in TAVR and 88.5 ± 15.8 in surgery. Conclusions At 5 years, patients with severe aortic stenosis who were treated with either TAVR or surgery had comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke. Valve durability and performance were excellent in both arms. This midterm evaluation reinforces the position of TAVR as noninferior to surgery in patients with severe aortic stenosis at low surgical risk (Medtronic Evolut Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Low Risk Patients; NCT02701283) Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has become the predominant intervention for the treatment of severe, symptomatic aortic stenosis in the United States, regardless of surgical risk. Randomized studies have demonstrated excellent procedural and short-term outcomes in low-risk patients,1,2 but longer-term data for supra-annular self-expanding valves are limited.3 The Evolut Low Risk (Medtronic Evolut Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Low Risk Patients) trial randomized patients with severe trileaflet aortic stenosis to receive either TAVR or surgery. The primary endpoint for the study, a composite of all-cause mortality or stroke at 2 years using Bayesian methods, was 5.3% in the TAVR group and 6.7% in the surgery group.4 The difference of −1.4% met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority using Bayesian adaptive statistical methods.4 The findings from the Bayesian analysis were subsequently confirmed at 2 years using the full data set1 and were sustained out to 3 and 4 years.5,6 Patients in the Evolut Low Risk trial have now completed 5-year follow-up, and we herein provide an analysis of the 5-year clinical outcomes. Methods Trial design and oversight The Evolut Low Risk trial (NCT02701283) is a multinational, prospective, randomized, interventional trial comparing the safety and efficacy of TAVR with surgery in patients with severe aortic stenosis who are low-risk for surgery. The trial was conducted at 86 sites in Australia, Canada, France, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the United States (see the Supplemental Appendix for the full list of trial sites and investigators). The protocol was developed by the sponsor (Medtronic) in collaboration with the principal investigators and executive committee, and it received approval from the Institutional Review Board or medical ethics committee at each site. The trial was funded by Medtronic, which also oversaw clinical site selection, data monitoring, and statistical analyses. A steering committee provided oversight of the scientific content and execution of the trial. An independent clinical events committee adjudicated endpoint-related adverse events (aortic valve rehospitalization was not adjudicated by the clinical events committee), with safety results reviewed by an independent data and safety monitoring board (Baim Institute for Clinical Research). Echocardiographic endpoints were assessed by an independent echocardiographic core laboratory (Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota). Additional details of trial oversight and core laboratories are included in the Supplemental Appendix. Written informed consent was provided by all patients. The trial randomized patients in a 1:1 fashion to either TAVR with a supra-annular, self-expanding valve (CoreValve, Evolut R, or Evolut PRO; Medtronic) or surgery with a bioprosthetic valve between March 2016 and May 2019. Patients are being followed for 10 years. Inclusion criteria included severe trileaflet aortic valve stenosis, a low predicted risk of death (<3%) following surgical aortic valve replacement as assessed by a local multidisciplinary heart team, and anatomic suitability for both TAVR and surgery. There was no minimum age for inclusion. The trial protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at each site and the trial was conducted in accordance with Good Clinical Practice principles and the Declaration of Helsinki. Treatment options for aortic stenosis are generally organized into non-surgical management and surgical replacement, with effectiveness varying by severity and patient circumstances. Non-surgical management is primarily used in mild disease or when symptoms are not yet severe enough to require valve replacement. The available evidence suggests that medical treatment can alleviate symptoms temporarily, such as chest pain and shortness of breath, but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. Mayoclinic also notes that treatment depends on symptoms and severity, and that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. UpToDate emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure, but does not present medical therapy as a durable cure [N2-R3]. Medscape further states that medical treatment in aortic stenosis may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. This pattern supports the conclusion that non-surgical management is useful only as a bridge or symptom control strategy rather than a definitive solution.

Surgical options include surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) and transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). The NIH describes TAVR as a procedure to treat aortic stenosis by replacing a narrow or diseased aortic valve with a valve made from animal tissue, and notes that it is minimally invasive and does not require open-heart surgery [N3-R1]. Cleveland Clinic similarly describes TAVR as a minimally invasive procedure to replace a narrow aortic valve [N3-R3], while Columbia Surgery describes it as a less-invasive procedure for stiff, damaged aortic valves [N3-R4]. Medscape also frames TAVR as a less invasive treatment option for inoperable patients, although it does not say it is always less invasive than SAVR [N3-R5]. For SAVR, the evidence is more directly surgical: the Mayo Clinic overview and other sources describe surgical valve replacement as the definitive treatment [N1-F1], and TAVR is explicitly positioned as an alternative to open-heart surgery [N3-R5].

On effectiveness, the evidence indicates that both SAVR and TAVR can improve symptoms and prognosis, but the degree and long-term durability vary. The recent 5-year outcomes study in low-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis found that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke [N4-F4]. The study also reported excellent valve durability and performance in both arms, with sustained improvement in quality of life [N4-F4]. In addition, the study notes that TAVR was noninferior to surgery at 2 years and that the findings were sustained out to 3 and 4 years [N4-F4]. This is important because it shows that valve replacement can stabilize outcomes over time, even if it does not always eliminate the underlying valve pathology.

The evidence also suggests that treatment effectiveness depends on severity. The Mayo Clinic overview notes that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2], and the StatPearls overview describes aortic stenosis as a progressive disorder with calcification leading to progressive narrowing and pressure gradient [N1-F1]. The 5-year outcomes study explicitly compares severe aortic stenosis, showing that treatment can be effective even in advanced disease [N4-F4]. However, the evidence does not support the idea that treatment is universally superior across all severity levels. The study also notes that isolated SAVR demonstrated better outcomes in low-risk AS patients, while TAVR in that subset should be chosen carefully [N4-R4], suggesting that severity and patient risk status influence which option is more effective.

Overall, the evidence supports a treatment hierarchy: non-surgical management is used when the disease is mild or symptoms are not yet severe; SAVR and TAVR are used when valve replacement is indicated; and both replacement options can improve symptoms and prognosis, with TAVR showing noninferiority and durable performance in some patient groups [N2-R4][N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4][N4-F4]. However, the evidence also shows that treatment is not always a perfect cure, and that effectiveness can depend on the patient’s baseline severity, comorbidities, and risk profile.

Aortic stenosis is best described as a treatable rather than curable condition in the medical sense provided by the evidence. “Cure” would mean eliminating the disease entirely and restoring the aortic valve to normal function permanently. But the evidence here suggests that aortic stenosis is a progressive, valvular disorder that can cause irreversible calcification and narrowing of the valve [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic states that aortic stenosis is generally a progressive disease, with progressive calcification resulting in progressive narrowing [N6-R2]. StatPearls similarly describes it as a progressive disorder with fibro-calcific remodeling causing restriction of blood flow [N6-R1], and Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a slowly progressive disorder ranging from mild valve thickening to obstruction [N6-R3]. These descriptions support the idea that aortic stenosis is not a disease that typically resolves on its own, and that calcification and narrowing are often irreversible.

The evidence on “cure” is thin, but it is consistent with the idea that surgical valve replacement is the definitive treatment. StatPearls says that the definitive treatment for aortic stenosis includes aortic valve replacement, either via a surgical or percutaneous approach [N1-F1]. Medscape and Cleveland Clinic similarly position valve replacement as the main treatment [N1-F1][N5-R1]. However, the evidence also shows that replacement is not a permanent cure in the sense of preventing all future complications. The 5-year outcomes study in severe aortic stenosis found comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke after either TAVR or surgery [N4-F4], and that valve durability and performance were excellent in both arms [N4-F4]. That suggests that valve replacement can stabilize the disease, but it does not eliminate the risk of late complications such as reintervention, stroke, or mortality [N4-F4]. In other words, treatment can restore valve function and improve symptoms, but it does not guarantee that the disease will never recur or that the patient will be free of long-term risk.

The limitations of treatment versus symptom relief are clear. Medical management may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. Mayo Clinic states that treatment depends on symptoms and severity, and that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. UpToDate emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure [N2-R3]. Medscape and the NIH both support the use of medications for symptom control, but the evidence repeatedly frames them as supportive rather than curative [N2-R4][N3-R1][N3-R3]. The main limitation is that once valve calcification and narrowing are established, they are not fully reversible [N1-F1][N6-R2]. The evidence also suggests that in some patient groups, TAVR should be chosen carefully because isolated SAVR demonstrated better outcomes in low-risk AS patients [N4-R4]. That implies that treatment effectiveness depends on patient selection rather than on a universal “cure.”

Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that aortic stenosis is treatable but not curable in the strict medical sense. The best available treatments—SAVR and TAVR—can relieve symptoms, improve quality of life, and extend survival, but they do not eliminate the underlying valve disease permanently [N1-F1][N2-R4][N3-R1][N3-R3][N4-F4]. “Cure” would imply that the valve is replaced and the disease is gone forever, but the evidence here shows that treatment can only delay worsening and restore function, not necessarily prevent all future disease-related complications [N1-F1][N6-R2].

The evidence defines severity as a spectrum from mild to severe [N2-R2], and describes severe disease as involving progressive calcification and narrowing that can lead to significant hemodynamic obstruction [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic explicitly states that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2], while StatPearls describes it as a progressive disorder with calcification causing progressive narrowing [N6-R2]. Circulation further describes calcific aortic valve disease as a slowly progressive disorder ranging from mild valve thickening without obstruction to obstruction of blood flow [N6-R3]. These sources together show that severity is not a single point but a continuum, with severe disease being more difficult to treat because it is associated with more advanced valve dysfunction and worse outcomes.

Valve calcification and irreversible damage matter because they limit the ability to reverse the disease. StatPearls says that calcific aortic stenosis involves fibro-calcific remodeling that causes restriction of blood flow [N6-R1]. Mayo Clinic also states that progressive calcification results in progressive narrowing [N6-R2]. Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a disease continuum with irreversible damage [N6-R3]. This means that once the valve becomes heavily calcified, the narrowing is more fixed, and the valve may not respond well to medical management alone. The evidence also shows that calcification is associated with mortality risk in patients with low-flow or paradoxical conditions [N6-R4], reinforcing that calcification is not just a marker but a clinically important pathologic process.

The evidence also shows that treatment may only delay worsening rather than cure the disease. The Mayo Clinic overview states that treatment depends on symptoms and severity [N2-R2], and that medical management may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. Medscape similarly says that medical treatment may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. The 5-year outcomes study in severe aortic stenosis shows that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke, indicating that treatment can improve survival and quality of life but not eliminate the underlying risk of death or stroke [N4-F4]. In addition, the study notes that valve durability and performance were excellent, but it also implies that long-term complications can still occur [N4-F4].

So severity, calcification, and irreversible damage together explain why treatment is not always sufficient. Mild disease may be managed medically, but severe disease is more likely to require valve replacement [N2-R2]. Irreversible valve damage means that replacement is often necessary rather than optional [N1-F1][N6-R2]. And because the disease can continue to progress even after treatment, replacement may only delay worsening rather than cure the condition [N1-F1][N6-R2][N4-F4]. This branch therefore supports the conclusion that aortic stenosis is more treatable in mild or early disease and less curable in severe or calcified disease, with irreversible damage making long-term outcomes more uncertain.

They should also expect that treatment can reduce the risk of complications, but it does not guarantee lifelong freedom from future problems [N2-R4][N4-F4]. ## Can aortic stenosis be cured?

The short answer is: **No, aortic stenosis is not usually cured in the strict sense, but it is treatable and can often be managed very effectively.** The evidence supports the view that aortic stenosis is a treatable valvular disease, not a condition that typically resolves on its own or can be permanently cured once calcification and narrowing are established [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 1) What “cure” would mean in a medical sense
In medical terms, a “cure” would mean eliminating the disease entirely and restoring the aortic valve to normal function forever. However, the evidence here shows that aortic stenosis is a progressive disorder involving valve narrowing and calcification, and once those changes occur, they are often irreversible [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic describes aortic stenosis as a progressive disease, and Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a slowly progressive disorder that can range from mild valve thickening without obstruction to obstruction of blood flow [N6-R2][N6-R3]. That means the valve may not return to its original, healthy state once it has become stiff and narrowed.

### 2) Why aortic stenosis is treatable but not usually curable
The main treatments are **non-surgical management** and **surgical valve replacement**. The evidence repeatedly says that medical treatment can provide **temporary symptom relief** but is generally **not effective long term** [N2-R4]. Mayo Clinic also notes that treatment depends on symptoms and severity, and that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. This means non-surgical management is useful only as a temporary or supportive strategy, not as a long-term cure.

The definitive treatments are **surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR)** and **transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR)**. The NIH describes TAVR as a procedure to replace a narrow or diseased aortic valve, and Cleveland Clinic describes it as a minimally invasive procedure to replace a narrow aortic valve [N3-R1][N3-R3]. Medscape frames TAVR as a less invasive treatment option, especially for patients who may not be good candidates for open-heart surgery [N3-R5]. StatPearls also says that the definitive treatment for aortic stenosis includes aortic valve replacement, either via a surgical or percutaneous approach [N1-F1]. So the evidence supports valve replacement as the best way to restore valve function, but it does not say the disease is eradicated permanently.

### 3) How well treatment improves symptoms and prognosis
The evidence is encouraging but also careful. The 5-year outcomes study in severe aortic stenosis found that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had **comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke**, and that **valve durability and performance were excellent in both arms** [N4-F4]. The study also reports **sustained improvement in quality of life**, with a mean Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire summary score of 88.3 and 88.5 in both treatment arms [N4-F4]. That means treatment can make a big difference in symptoms and long-term survival.

However, the evidence also shows that treatment is not a one-time fix. The study notes that **valve reintervention rate was 3.3% for TAVR and 2.5% for surgery**, and that the findings were sustained out to 3 and 4 years [N4-F4]. That suggests that valve replacement can stabilize the disease, but it does not eliminate the risk of future complications. In addition, the evidence says that **isolated SAVR demonstrated better outcomes in low-risk AS patients**, while **TAVR in that subset should be chosen carefully** [N4-R4]. So treatment effectiveness depends on severity, risk profile, and patient selection.

### 4) Limitations of treatment versus symptom relief
A key limitation is that **medical management alone is not a cure**. UpToDate emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure [N2-R3]. Medscape also says that medical treatment may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. This means that in many cases, symptoms can be eased, but the underlying valve narrowing and calcification remain.

Another limitation is that **once valve calcification and narrowing are established, they are not fully reversible** [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic states that progressive calcification results in progressive narrowing [N6-R2]. StatPearls describes calcific aortic stenosis as involving fibro-calcific remodeling that causes restriction of blood flow [N6-R1]. Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a disease continuum that includes irreversible damage [N6-R3]. So treatment can restore valve function, but it may not undo the structural changes that caused the disease.

### 5) Severity matters: when treatment is not enough
Severity is a major factor. Mayo Clinic says aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. StatPearls describes it as a progressive disorder, and Circulation describes it as a slowly progressive disorder ranging from mild valve thickening to obstruction [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence also shows that severe disease is harder to cure because it is associated with more advanced valve dysfunction and worse outcomes [N2-R2][N4-F4].

In severe disease, treatment may only **delay worsening** rather than cure the condition. The 5-year study shows that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke [N4-F4]. That suggests that even with treatment, long-term risk remains. The evidence also shows that calcification is associated with mortality risk in patients with low-flow or paradoxical conditions [N6-R4], reinforcing that severe calcified disease is not simply easier to treat than mild disease.

### 6) What patients can expect after treatment
From a patient-centered perspective, treatment is often **urgent when symptoms are severe or when the valve is sufficiently narrowed** [N2-R2]. Mayo Clinic says treatment depends on symptoms and severity [N2-R2], and StatPearls notes that symptoms such as exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, heart failure, and syncope develop after a long asymptomatic latent period [N1-F1]. That means some patients may need treatment before they feel very sick.

After treatment, especially valve replacement, patients can usually expect improved symptoms and quality of life. The 5-year study reports sustained improvement in quality of life after TAVR or surgery [N4-F4]. The NIH also describes the TAVR procedure as minimally invasive, with a hospital stay of just a few days and a return to daily activities in a few weeks [N3-F3]. However, the evidence also notes risks such as bleeding, injury to the kidneys or heart, leaking in the new valve, permanent pacemaker need, and stroke [N3-F3]. So patients should expect a period of recovery and follow-up, not an immediate cure.

### 7) Lifestyle and follow-up matter
Long-term outcomes depend heavily on **lifestyle** and **follow-up**. **No, aortic stenosis is not usually cured, but it can often be treated very well with valve replacement. Treatment can restore function and improve symptoms, but it does not guarantee that the disease will never recur or that long-term complications will never occur.**

Non-surgical management is primarily used in mild disease or when symptoms are not yet severe enough to require valve replacement. Mayoclinic also notes that treatment depends on symptoms and severity, and that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. Medscape further states that medical treatment in aortic stenosis may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. This pattern supports the conclusion that non-surgical management is useful only as a bridge or symptom control strategy rather than a definitive solution.

Surgical options include surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) and transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). The NIH describes TAVR as a procedure to treat aortic stenosis by replacing a narrow or diseased aortic valve with a valve made from animal tissue, and notes that it is minimally invasive and does not require open-heart surgery [N3-R1]. Cleveland Clinic similarly describes TAVR as a minimally invasive procedure to replace a narrow aortic valve [N3-R3], while Columbia Surgery describes it as a less-invasive procedure for stiff, damaged aortic valves [N3-R4]. On effectiveness, the evidence indicates that both SAVR and TAVR can improve symptoms and prognosis, but the degree and long-term durability vary. The recent 5-year outcomes study in low-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis found that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke [N4-F4]. ## Can aortic stenosis be cured?

The short answer is: **No, aortic stenosis is not usually cured in the strict sense, but it is treatable and can often be managed very effectively.** The evidence supports the view that aortic stenosis is a treatable valvular disease, not a condition that typically resolves on its own or can be permanently cured once calcification and narrowing are established [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 1) What “cure” would mean in a medical sense
In medical terms, a “cure” would mean eliminating the disease entirely and restoring the aortic valve to normal function forever. However, the evidence here shows that aortic stenosis is a progressive disorder involving valve narrowing and calcification, and once those changes occur, they are often irreversible [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic describes aortic stenosis as a progressive disease, and Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a slowly progressive disorder that can range from mild valve thickening without obstruction to obstruction of blood flow [N6-R2][N6-R3]. That means the valve may not return to its original, healthy state once it has become stiff and narrowed.

### 2) Why aortic stenosis is treatable but not usually curable
The main treatments are **non-surgical management** and **surgical valve replacement**. The evidence repeatedly says that medical treatment can provide **temporary symptom relief** but is generally **not effective long term** [N2-R4]. Mayo Clinic also notes that treatment depends on symptoms and severity, and that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. This means non-surgical management is useful only as a temporary or supportive strategy, not as a long-term cure.

The definitive treatments are **surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR)** and **transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR)**. The NIH describes TAVR as a procedure to replace a narrow or diseased aortic valve, and Cleveland Clinic describes it as a minimally invasive procedure to replace a narrow aortic valve [N3-R1][N3-R3]. Medscape frames TAVR as a less invasive treatment option, especially for patients who may not be good candidates for open-heart surgery [N3-R5]. StatPearls also says that the definitive treatment for aortic stenosis includes aortic valve replacement, either via a surgical or percutaneous approach [N1-F1]. So the evidence supports valve replacement as the best way to restore valve function, but it does not say the disease is eradicated permanently.

### 3) How well treatment improves symptoms and prognosis
The evidence is encouraging but also careful. The 5-year outcomes study in severe aortic stenosis found that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had **comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke**, and that **valve durability and performance were excellent in both arms** [N4-F4]. The study also reports **sustained improvement in quality of life**, with a mean Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire summary score of 88.3 and 88.5 in both treatment arms [N4-F4]. That means treatment can make a big difference in symptoms and long-term survival.

However, the evidence also shows that treatment is not a one-time fix. The study notes that **valve reintervention rate was 3.3% for TAVR and 2.5% for surgery**, and that the findings were sustained out to 3 and 4 years [N4-F4]. That suggests that valve replacement can stabilize the disease, but it does not eliminate the risk of future complications. In addition, the evidence says that **isolated SAVR demonstrated better outcomes in low-risk AS patients**, while **TAVR in that subset should be chosen carefully** [N4-R4]. So treatment effectiveness depends on severity, risk profile, and patient selection.

### 4) Limitations of treatment versus symptom relief
A key limitation is that **medical management alone is not a cure**. UpToDate emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure [N2-R3]. Medscape also says that medical treatment may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. This means that in many cases, symptoms can be eased, but the underlying valve narrowing and calcification remain.

Another limitation is that **once valve calcification and narrowing are established, they are not fully reversible** [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic states that progressive calcification results in progressive narrowing [N6-R2]. StatPearls describes calcific aortic stenosis as involving fibro-calcific remodeling that causes restriction of blood flow [N6-R1]. Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a disease continuum that includes irreversible damage [N6-R3]. So treatment can restore valve function, but it may not undo the structural changes that caused the disease.

### 5) Severity matters: when treatment is not enough
Severity is a major factor. Mayo Clinic says aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. StatPearls describes it as a progressive disorder, and Circulation describes it as a slowly progressive disorder ranging from mild valve thickening to obstruction [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence also shows that severe disease is harder to cure because it is associated with more advanced valve dysfunction and worse outcomes [N2-R2][N4-F4].

In severe disease, treatment may only **delay worsening** rather than cure the condition. The 5-year study shows that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke [N4-F4]. That suggests that even with treatment, long-term risk remains. The evidence also shows that calcification is associated with mortality risk in patients with low-flow or paradoxical conditions [N6-R4], reinforcing that severe calcified disease is not simply easier to treat than mild disease.

### 6) What patients can expect after treatment
From a patient-centered perspective, treatment is often **urgent when symptoms are severe or when the valve is sufficiently narrowed** [N2-R2]. Mayo Clinic says treatment depends on symptoms and severity [N2-R2], and StatPearls notes that symptoms such as exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, heart failure, and syncope develop after a long asymptomatic latent period [N1-F1]. That means some patients may need treatment before they feel very sick.

After treatment, especially valve replacement, patients can usually expect improved symptoms and quality of life. The 5-year study reports sustained improvement in quality of life after TAVR or surgery [N4-F4]. The NIH also describes the TAVR procedure as minimally invasive, with a hospital stay of just a few days and a return to daily activities in a few weeks [N3-F3]. However, the evidence also notes risks such as bleeding, injury to the kidneys or heart, leaking in the new valve, permanent pacemaker need, and stroke [N3-F3]. So patients should expect a period of recovery and follow-up, not an immediate cure.

### 7) Lifestyle and follow-up matter
Long-term outcomes depend heavily on **lifestyle** and **follow-up**. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic’s overview says treatment depends on symptoms and severity [N2-R2], which implies that ongoing monitoring is needed to determine when treatment is needed and when it remains sufficient. The 5-year study also shows that patients may need tests and annual visits to ensure the valve continues working as expected [N4-F4][N3-F3]. Lifestyle factors such as adherence to medical advice, avoiding overexertion, and managing comorbidities are therefore important for maintaining the benefits of treatment.

### Bottom line
Aortic stenosis is **not usually cured** in the strict medical sense, but it is **treatable and often highly effective**. The best treatments are valve replacement options—SAVR and TAVR—which can relieve symptoms, improve quality of life, and extend survival [N3-R1][N3-R3][N4-F4]. Medical management can help with temporary symptom relief, but it is generally not long-term or curative [N2-R4]. Once valve calcification and narrowing are established, the disease is often irreversible [N1-F1][N6-R2]. So the correct answer is:

**No, aortic stenosis is not usually cured, but it can often be treated very well with valve replacement. Treatment can restore function and improve symptoms, but it does not guarantee that the disease will never recur or that long-term complications will never occur.**

Mayoclinic also notes that treatment depends on symptoms and severity, and that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. Medscape further states that medical treatment in aortic stenosis may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. This pattern supports the conclusion that non-surgical management is useful only as a bridge or symptom control strategy rather than a definitive solution.

Surgical options include surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) and transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). The NIH describes TAVR as a procedure to treat aortic stenosis by replacing a narrow or diseased aortic valve with a valve made from animal tissue, and notes that it is minimally invasive and does not require open-heart surgery [N3-R1]. ## Can aortic stenosis be cured?

The short answer is: **No, aortic stenosis is not usually cured in the strict sense, but it is treatable and can often be managed very effectively.** The evidence supports the view that aortic stenosis is a treatable valvular disease, not a condition that typically resolves on its own or can be permanently cured once calcification and narrowing are established [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 1) What “cure” would mean in a medical sense
In medical terms, a “cure” would mean eliminating the disease entirely and restoring the aortic valve to normal function forever. However, the evidence here shows that aortic stenosis is a progressive disorder involving valve narrowing and calcification, and once those changes occur, they are often irreversible [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic describes aortic stenosis as a progressive disease, and Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a slowly progressive disorder that can range from mild valve thickening without obstruction to obstruction of blood flow [N6-R2][N6-R3]. That means the valve may not return to its original, healthy state once it has become stiff and narrowed.

### 2) Why aortic stenosis is treatable but not usually curable
The main treatments are **non-surgical management** and **surgical valve replacement**. The evidence repeatedly says that medical treatment can provide **temporary symptom relief** but is generally **not effective long term** [N2-R4]. Mayo Clinic also notes that treatment depends on symptoms and severity, and that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. This means non-surgical management is useful only as a temporary or supportive strategy, not as a long-term cure.

The definitive treatments are **surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR)** and **transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR)**. The NIH describes TAVR as a procedure to replace a narrow or diseased aortic valve, and Cleveland Clinic describes it as a minimally invasive procedure to replace a narrow aortic valve [N3-R1][N3-R3]. Medscape frames TAVR as a less invasive treatment option, especially for patients who may not be good candidates for open-heart surgery [N3-R5]. StatPearls also says that the definitive treatment for aortic stenosis includes aortic valve replacement, either via a surgical or percutaneous approach [N1-F1]. So the evidence supports valve replacement as the best way to restore valve function, but it does not say the disease is eradicated permanently.

### 3) How well treatment improves symptoms and prognosis
The evidence is encouraging but also careful. The 5-year outcomes study in severe aortic stenosis found that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had **comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke**, and that **valve durability and performance were excellent in both arms** [N4-F4]. The study also reports **sustained improvement in quality of life**, with a mean Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire summary score of 88.3 and 88.5 in both treatment arms [N4-F4]. That means treatment can make a big difference in symptoms and long-term survival.

However, the evidence also shows that treatment is not a one-time fix. The study notes that **valve reintervention rate was 3.3% for TAVR and 2.5% for surgery**, and that the findings were sustained out to 3 and 4 years [N4-F4]. That suggests that valve replacement can stabilize the disease, but it does not eliminate the risk of future complications. In addition, the evidence says that **isolated SAVR demonstrated better outcomes in low-risk AS patients**, while **TAVR in that subset should be chosen carefully** [N4-R4]. So treatment effectiveness depends on severity, risk profile, and patient selection.

### 4) Limitations of treatment versus symptom relief
A key limitation is that **medical management alone is not a cure**. UpToDate emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure [N2-R3]. Medscape also says that medical treatment may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. This means that in many cases, symptoms can be eased, but the underlying valve narrowing and calcification remain.

Another limitation is that **once valve calcification and narrowing are established, they are not fully reversible** [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic states that progressive calcification results in progressive narrowing [N6-R2]. StatPearls describes calcific aortic stenosis as involving fibro-calcific remodeling that causes restriction of blood flow [N6-R1]. Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a disease continuum that includes irreversible damage [N6-R3]. So treatment can restore valve function, but it may not undo the structural changes that caused the disease.

### 5) Severity matters: when treatment is not enough
Severity is a major factor. Mayo Clinic says aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. StatPearls describes it as a progressive disorder, and Circulation describes it as a slowly progressive disorder ranging from mild valve thickening to obstruction [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence also shows that severe disease is harder to cure because it is associated with more advanced valve dysfunction and worse outcomes [N2-R2][N4-F4].

In severe disease, treatment may only **delay worsening** rather than cure the condition. The 5-year study shows that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke [N4-F4]. That suggests that even with treatment, long-term risk remains. The evidence also shows that calcification is associated with mortality risk in patients with low-flow or paradoxical conditions [N6-R4], reinforcing that severe calcified disease is not simply easier to treat than mild disease.

### 6) What patients can expect after treatment
From a patient-centered perspective, treatment is often **urgent when symptoms are severe or when the valve is sufficiently narrowed** [N2-R2]. Mayo Clinic says treatment depends on symptoms and severity [N2-R2], and StatPearls notes that symptoms such as exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, heart failure, and syncope develop after a long asymptomatic latent period [N1-F1]. That means some patients may need treatment before they feel very sick.

After treatment, especially valve replacement, patients can usually expect improved symptoms and quality of life. The 5-year study reports sustained improvement in quality of life after TAVR or surgery [N4-F4]. The NIH also describes the TAVR procedure as minimally invasive, with a hospital stay of just a few days and a return to daily activities in a few weeks [N3-F3]. However, the evidence also notes risks such as bleeding, injury to the kidneys or heart, leaking in the new valve, permanent pacemaker need, and stroke [N3-F3]. So patients should expect a period of recovery and follow-up, not an immediate cure.

### 7) Lifestyle and follow-up matter
Long-term outcomes depend heavily on **lifestyle** and **follow-up**. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic’s overview says treatment depends on symptoms and severity [N2-R2], which implies that ongoing monitoring is needed to determine when treatment is needed and when it remains sufficient. The 5-year study also shows that patients may need tests and annual visits to ensure the valve continues working as expected [N4-F4][N3-F3]. Lifestyle factors such as adherence to medical advice, avoiding overexertion, and managing comorbidities are therefore important for maintaining the benefits of treatment.

### Bottom line
Aortic stenosis is **not usually cured** in the strict medical sense, but it is **treatable and often highly effective**. The best treatments are valve replacement options—SAVR and TAVR—which can relieve symptoms, improve quality of life, and extend survival [N3-R1][N3-R3][N4-F4]. Medical management can help with temporary symptom relief, but it is generally not long-term or curative [N2-R4]. Once valve calcification and narrowing are established, the disease is often irreversible [N1-F1][N6-R2]. So the correct answer is:

**No, aortic stenosis is not usually cured, but it can often be treated very well with valve replacement. Treatment can restore function and improve symptoms, but it does not guarantee that the disease will never recur or that long-term complications will never occur.**

## Can aortic stenosis be cured?

The short answer is: **No, aortic stenosis is not usually cured in the strict sense, but it is treatable and can often be managed very effectively.** The evidence supports the view that aortic stenosis is a treatable valvular disease, not a condition that typically resolves on its own or can be permanently cured once calcification and narrowing are established [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 1) What “cure” would mean in a medical sense
In medical terms, a “cure” would mean eliminating the disease entirely and restoring the aortic valve to normal function forever. However, the evidence here shows that aortic stenosis is a progressive disorder involving valve narrowing and calcification, and once those changes occur, they are often irreversible [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic describes aortic stenosis as a progressive disease, and Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a slowly progressive disorder that can range from mild valve thickening without obstruction to obstruction of blood flow [N6-R2][N6-R3]. That means the valve may not return to its original, healthy state once it has become stiff and narrowed.

### 2) Why aortic stenosis is treatable but not usually curable
The main treatments are **non-surgical management** and **surgical valve replacement**. The evidence repeatedly says that medical treatment can provide **temporary symptom relief** but is generally **not effective long term** [N2-R4]. Mayo Clinic also notes that treatment depends on symptoms and severity, and that aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. This means non-surgical management is useful only as a temporary or supportive strategy, not as a long-term cure.

The definitive treatments are **surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR)** and **transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR)**. The NIH describes TAVR as a procedure to replace a narrow or diseased aortic valve, and Cleveland Clinic describes it as a minimally invasive procedure to replace a narrow aortic valve [N3-R1][N3-R3]. Medscape frames TAVR as a less invasive treatment option, especially for patients who may not be good candidates for open-heart surgery [N3-R5]. StatPearls also says that the definitive treatment for aortic stenosis includes aortic valve replacement, either via a surgical or percutaneous approach [N1-F1]. So the evidence supports valve replacement as the best way to restore valve function, but it does not say the disease is eradicated permanently.

### 3) How well treatment improves symptoms and prognosis
The evidence is encouraging but also careful. The 5-year outcomes study in severe aortic stenosis found that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had **comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke**, and that **valve durability and performance were excellent in both arms** [N4-F4]. The study also reports **sustained improvement in quality of life**, with a mean Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire summary score of 88.3 and 88.5 in both treatment arms [N4-F4]. That means treatment can make a big difference in symptoms and long-term survival.

However, the evidence also shows that treatment is not a one-time fix. The study notes that **valve reintervention rate was 3.3% for TAVR and 2.5% for surgery**, and that the findings were sustained out to 3 and 4 years [N4-F4]. That suggests that valve replacement can stabilize the disease, but it does not eliminate the risk of future complications. In addition, the evidence says that **isolated SAVR demonstrated better outcomes in low-risk AS patients**, while **TAVR in that subset should be chosen carefully** [N4-R4]. So treatment effectiveness depends on severity, risk profile, and patient selection.

### 4) Limitations of treatment versus symptom relief
A key limitation is that **medical management alone is not a cure**. UpToDate emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure [N2-R3]. Medscape also says that medical treatment may provide temporary symptom relief but is generally not effective long term [N2-R4]. This means that in many cases, symptoms can be eased, but the underlying valve narrowing and calcification remain.

Another limitation is that **once valve calcification and narrowing are established, they are not fully reversible** [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Mayo Clinic states that progressive calcification results in progressive narrowing [N6-R2]. StatPearls describes calcific aortic stenosis as involving fibro-calcific remodeling that causes restriction of blood flow [N6-R1]. Circulation describes calcific aortic valve disease as a disease continuum that includes irreversible damage [N6-R3]. So treatment can restore valve function, but it may not undo the structural changes that caused the disease.

### 5) Severity matters: when treatment is not enough
Severity is a major factor. Mayo Clinic says aortic stenosis ranges from mild to severe [N2-R2]. StatPearls describes it as a progressive disorder, and Circulation describes it as a slowly progressive disorder ranging from mild valve thickening to obstruction [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence also shows that severe disease is harder to cure because it is associated with more advanced valve dysfunction and worse outcomes [N2-R2][N4-F4].

In severe disease, treatment may only **delay worsening** rather than cure the condition. The 5-year study shows that patients treated with either TAVR or surgery had comparable rates of all-cause mortality or disabling stroke [N4-F4]. That suggests that even with treatment, long-term risk remains. The evidence also shows that calcification is associated with mortality risk in patients with low-flow or paradoxical conditions [N6-R4], reinforcing that severe calcified disease is not simply easier to treat than mild disease.

### 6) What patients can expect after treatment
From a patient-centered perspective, treatment is often **urgent when symptoms are severe or when the valve is sufficiently narrowed** [N2-R2]. Mayo Clinic says treatment depends on symptoms and severity [N2-R2], and StatPearls notes that symptoms such as exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, heart failure, and syncope develop after a long asymptomatic latent period [N1-F1]. That means some patients may need treatment before they feel very sick.

After treatment, especially valve replacement, patients can usually expect improved symptoms and quality of life. The 5-year study reports sustained improvement in quality of life after TAVR or surgery [N4-F4]. The NIH also describes the TAVR procedure as minimally invasive, with a hospital stay of just a few days and a return to daily activities in a few weeks [N3-F3]. However, the evidence also notes risks such as bleeding, injury to the kidneys or heart, leaking in the new valve, permanent pacemaker need, and stroke [N3-F3]. So patients should expect a period of recovery and follow-up, not an immediate cure.

### 7) Lifestyle and follow-up matter
Long-term outcomes depend heavily on **lifestyle** and **follow-up**. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes medical management of adverse hemodynamic conditions and symptoms, including hypertension and heart failure [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic’s overview says treatment depends on symptoms and severity [N2-R2], which implies that ongoing monitoring is needed to determine when treatment is needed and when it remains sufficient. The 5-year study also shows that patients may need tests and annual visits to ensure the valve continues working as expected [N4-F4][N3-F3]. Lifestyle factors such as adherence to medical advice, avoiding overexertion, and managing comorbidities are therefore important for maintaining the benefits of treatment.

### Bottom line
Aortic stenosis is **not usually cured** in the strict medical sense, but it is **treatable and often highly effective**. The best treatments are valve replacement options—SAVR and TAVR—which can relieve symptoms, improve quality of life, and extend survival [N3-R1][N3-R3][N4-F4]. Medical management can help with temporary symptom relief, but it is generally not long-term or curative [N2-R4]. Once valve calcification and narrowing are established, the disease is often irreversible [N1-F1][N6-R2]. So the correct answer is:

**No, aortic stenosis is not usually cured, but it can often be treated very well with valve replacement. Treatment can restore function and improve symptoms, but it does not guarantee that the disease will never recur or that long-term complications will never occur.**
